title: Binary Tree Paths
description: Return every root-to-leaf path in a binary tree as arrow-joined strings, using backtracking over a shared path buffer.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the root of a binary tree, return all root-to-leaf paths, each formatted as a string with node values joined by "->", such as "1->2->5". Order of the returned paths does not matter.

blocks.caption: A shared path buffer records the current descent; a leaf completes one path, and popping before returning keeps sibling paths independent.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","root (binary tree, at least one node)"],["Path format","Node values joined by \"->\", e.g. \"1->2->5\""],["Output","All root-to-leaf paths, any order"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Enumerating every root-to-leaf path is a classic backtracking-over-a-tree problem: maintain a single shared path buffer, append the current node before descending, record a complete path at each leaf, and remove the current node from the buffer before returning to the parent, so sibling subtrees never see it.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The append-before-descend, remove-after-return pattern is the general backtracking template applied to tree traversal instead of array/string generation.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a hiker keeping a running trail log as they descend a tree of trails. Each stop is written into the log. At a dead end (leaf), the entire log so far is recorded as one completed route. Before backtracking up to try a different branch, the current stop is erased from the log, since it should not appear in trails explored from a sibling branch.

blocks.caption: A stop is erased from the log before backtracking to try a different branch.

items: Append the current node's value to a shared path buffer before recursing into its children.
At a leaf (no children), join the buffer into one arrow-separated string and record it as a complete path.
After exploring both children (or immediately at a leaf), remove the current node from the buffer before returning, so it does not leak into other paths.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
root = [1,2,3,null,5] (node 2 has a right child 5, no left child; node 3 is a leaf).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Path buffer","Action"],"rows":[["Visit 1","[1]","not a leaf, descend left"],["Visit 2","[1, 2]","not a leaf (has right child 5), descend right"],["Visit 5","[1, 2, 5]","leaf, record \"1->2->5\""],["Backtrack to 2, then to 1","[1]","pop 2 and 5, now descend right from 1"],["Visit 3","[1, 3]","leaf, record \"1->3\""]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The recorded paths are ["1->2->5", "1->3"], matching the expected output exactly.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct approach recursively computes the list of paths for the left subtree and the right subtree separately, then prepends the current node's value to each returned path. This is correct and avoids any shared mutable state, but creates many small intermediate string lists during the recursion.
Using one shared path buffer, appended to and popped from as the recursion descends and returns, avoids allocating new lists at every level, only building a full path string once, at each leaf.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively compute the paths of the left and right subtrees independently, then prepend the current node's value to each returned path string.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2) worst case","Prepending to every returned path string at every level can repeatedly copy substrings"],["Space","O(n^2) worst case","Many intermediate path lists and string copies across the recursion"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rebuilding and prepending to path strings at every level of the recursion is less efficient than maintaining one shared buffer.
8. Optimize the Solution

Maintain one shared path buffer (a list, appended to and popped from). Descend the tree, appending each node's value; at a leaf, join the buffer into a string and record it; after visiting both children (or immediately at a leaf), pop the current node off before returning to the caller.

items: Append the current node to the shared path buffer.
At a leaf, join the buffer with "->" and record the result.
Otherwise recurse into both children; either way, pop the current node from the buffer before returning.

10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, prepend at every level","O(n^2) worst case","O(n^2) worst case"],["Optimized, shared path buffer","O(n^2) worst case (joining strings at leaves)","O(n) for the buffer, plus recursion stack"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Both share the same worst-case string-building cost (a skewed tree's single path has length n, joined once per leaf); the optimized version avoids REPEATED prepending at every intermediate level.
11. Key Takeaways

items: A shared, mutable path buffer avoids repeated string/list copying compared to returning and merging separate child results.
The append-before-descend, pop-after-return pattern is the general backtracking template, here applied to tree paths instead of combinatorial generation.
A leaf is the natural "record a complete result" point in any root-to-leaf enumeration problem.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Binary Tree Paths is solved with backtracking over a shared path buffer: each node is appended before descending, a leaf records the buffer as a complete arrow-joined path, and the node is popped before returning to the parent, ensuring sibling subtrees never see it. This visits every node exactly once while cleanly enumerating all root-to-leaf paths.
